title: Diagnosis of isolated hepatic tuberculosis in an immunocompetent individual: a case report and review of misdiagnosed cases
case_text: A 44-year-old woman presented with complaints of abdominal pain for the past 2 months. The patient's abdominal pain was intermittent, lasting from several minutes to several hours. It was accompanied by a decreased appetite, fever, and night sweats. However, there were no symptoms of nausea, vomiting, changes in bowel movements, chills, or cough with sputum production. The patient was born and currently resides in Luzhou City, Sichuan Province, China. She is a company clerk and denies any history of contact with animals or tuberculosis. She also reports no past medical history of liver disease, tuberculosis, or acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS). In the past year, she had not experienced any weight loss or traveled outside of Luzhou. She was dyspneic (RR = 20 breaths/min), had a temperature of 36.5  C, a heart rate of 70 beats per minute, blood pressure of 118/78 (normal range, 60-90/90-140) mmHg, and a 33% oxygen saturation on room air at the time of admission. Abdominal examination revealed periumbilical and right lower abdominal wall tenderness and rebound pain. The rest of the system examination was unremarkable. The chest computed tomography (CT) was normal. The contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan shows a small amount of ascites in the lesser omentum sac and the abdominal and pelvic cavities, with the pelvic cavity being the main site. The greater omentum, mesentery, and peritoneum are extensively thickened, with some areas showing nodular thickening. These are all manifestations of tuberculous peritonitis. The contrast-enhanced CT also reveals a round, low-density, non-enhancing shadow in the right anterior lobe of the liver, with a diameter of approximately 0.8 cm. There is a patchy enhancement in the left medial lobe of the liver during the arterial phase, and the enhancement is consistent with the surrounding liver parenchyma during the venous phase. The hepatic CT showed an irregular mass of approximately 4.1 cm x 3.1 cm in the right anterior space of the liver, part of which invaded the right anterior lobe of the liver (Figure 1a). The findings are consistent with an infection complicated by abscess formation involving the anterior segment of the right hepatic lobe. The right lobe of the liver's ultrasound revealed a cystic dark region measuring 3.7 cm x 2.1 cm (Figure 1b). To confirm the diagnosis, we performed a liver biopsy. Ultrasound-guided biopsy of the lesion was done, which showed chronic granulomatous inflammation suggestive of tuberculosis (Figure 1c). The tuberculin test was positive. TB-DNA real-time PCR performed on the aspirated pus was positive, confirming the presence of M. tuberculosis complex DNA. Her total leucocyte count was 7.01 (normal range, 3.5-9.5) x 109/L, neutrophil count was 5.56 (normal range, 1.8-6.3) x 109/L, platelet count was 229 (normal range, 100-350) x 109/L, C-reactive protein (CRP) level was 10.65 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 33 mm3. The renal function and electrolyte tests showed urea, 5 (normal range, 3.1-8.0) mmol/L; uric acid, 231 (normal range, 208-428) mumol/L; glomerular filtration rate, 100 (normal range, >=90) mL/min; creatinine, 72 (normal range, 57-97) mumol/L; potassium, 4.15 (normal range, 3.5-5.3) mmol/L; sodium, 140 (normal range, 137-147) mmol/L; and chloride, 105.2 (normal range, 99-110) mmol/L. The liver function tests showed alanine aminotransferase, 80 (normal range, 9-50) U/L; aspartate aminotransferase, 78 (normal range, 15-40) U/L; total bilirubin, 17 (normal range, 0-26) U/L; direct bilirubin, 8.6 (normal range, 0-8) U/L; indirect bilirubin, 8.4 (normal range, 0-20) U/L; and albumin, 35 (normal range, 40-55) g/L. Blood culture was negative. The carcinoembryonic antigen, CA-19.9, CA-125, and a-fetoprotein serum tumor markers were all within normal limits. The HIV test was negative. She was diagnosed with hepatic tuberculosis and tuberculous peritonitis. Anti-tuberculous medication (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide) was initiated for the patient. The abscess's size had increased on the abdominal ultrasonography performed 1 month after the diagnosis (Figure 1d). Abdominal ultrasound revealed a 4.4 cm x 3.4 cm area of heterogeneous echogenicity in the anterior segment of the right hepatic lobe, with ill-defined borders, hypoechoic areas, and internal septations. After discharge, the patient continued to be managed and followed up as an outpatient, but she took herself to a specialized infectious-disease hospital immediately after this repeat ultrasound. During the subsequent period, telephone follow-up indicated that the patient continued anti-tuberculosis therapy (the specific regimen was not documented), with symptoms gradually improving and essentially resolving after 6 months.

Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Tuberculosis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: hepatic tuberculosis and tuberculous peritonitis
